ordered.title: Common questions about engine replacement costs

blocks.question: How much does engine replacement cost in the UK? +
blocks.answer: Engine replacement costs range from £1,700 to £7,350+ depending on vehicle type and condition. Most owners pay between £2,500 and £4,500 for a fitted reconditioned engine. Supply-only costs start from £1,500 for used and £2,100 for reconditioned.

blocks.question: What's the difference between used, reconditioned, rebuilt, and new? +
blocks.answer: Used: from a donor vehicle, unknown history. Reconditioned: cleaned, worn parts replaced, tested. Rebuilt: stripped and rebuilt with a mixture of new and serviceable parts. Remanufactured: factory-spec rebuild with strict tolerances. New: brand new from manufacturer. See the table above for costs and best-use cases.

blocks.question: Is it cheaper to repair or replace an engine? +
blocks.answer: If damage is isolated (timing chain rattle caught early, head gasket seepage), targeted repair may be cheaper. Advanced failure (rod knock, snapped timing belt on interference engine) often makes replacement more cost-effective. → Repair vs Replacement comparison

blocks.question: Does engine replacement cost include fitting? +
blocks.answer: Not always. Always confirm with your supplier. Our price tables show supply-only and fitted costs separately. Fitting typically adds £800-£2,200 depending on engine type and labour rates.

blocks.question: How long does an engine replacement take? +
blocks.answer: From quote request to completion, the average is 5.2 days [EM-VERIFIED]. Fitting labour typically takes 1-3 days depending on engine complexity. Allow 2-5 days for engine sourcing and delivery.

blocks.question: What warranty comes with a replacement engine? +
blocks.answer: Used engines: 1-6 months. Reconditioned: 6-12 months. Rebuilt and remanufactured: 12-24 months. New OEM: 12-24 months. Engines Market does not provide warranties - we connect you with suppliers who do. Always check the supplier's warranty terms in writing.

blocks.question: Can I fit a used engine from a different vehicle? +
blocks.answer: Yes, but you need the exact same engine code and often the same variant to ensure compatibility. Your supplier will match the engine code to your vehicle's VIN. Never assume a similar engine will fit.

blocks.question: What happens to my old engine? +
blocks.answer: Your old engine is typically collected and scrapped by the supplier or garage. This is usually included in the fitting cost. Some suppliers may offer a discount if your old engine has salvageable parts (e.g., cylinder head, turbo, injectors).

blocks.question: Should I replace the clutch/DMF at the same time? +
blocks.answer: If you have a manual gearbox and the engine is out, absolutely consider it. The labour cost to replace a clutch/DMF is much higher if done separately. Many owners regret not doing it "while the engine is out."

blocks.question: Can I drive with a failing engine? +
blocks.answer: It depends. If you hear a deep knock, see the oil pressure warning light, or notice significant power loss - stop driving immediately. Continuing will cause more damage and increase the repair cost.

blocks.question: How do I know if my car is worth repairing? +
blocks.answer: A rough rule: if the replacement cost exceeds 60% of your vehicle's market value, consider scrapping. However, rare, collectable, or sentimental vehicles may justify spending above this threshold.

blocks.question: What hidden costs should I watch out for? +
blocks.answer: Common hidden costs: clutch/DMF, water pump, timing belt/chain, air-con regas, delivery charges, pallet return fees, and unforeseen repairs discovered during fitting. Always ask for a written breakdown.

blocks.question: Is engine replacement covered by car insurance? +
blocks.answer: Only if you have a comprehensive policy and the damage is from an insured event (accident, fire, theft). Mechanical failure and wear-and-tear are not covered by standard insurance.

blocks.question: Do I need to tell my insurer about an engine replacement? +
blocks.answer: Yes. Any major mechanical change must be declared to your insurer. Failure to do so could invalidate your insurance policy. The new engine code and number should also be recorded on your V5C (logbook).
